rows.question: Explain CUDA warps.
rows.answer: A CUDA warp is a group of 32 GPU threads that execute instructions together. Threads in a warp can work on different data, but if they take different branches, the GPU executes the different paths with only the relevant threads active, which can reduce efficiency. For good performance, minimize branch divergence and have neighboring threads access neighboring memory locations.

rows.name: hour-1-spoken-why-warps
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Warps let the GPU execute one instruction across 32 threads efficiently. When threads take different branches, the warp must execute the different paths with only the relevant threads active, reducing useful work per instruction. Neighboring threads accessing neighboring memory locations also lets the GPU combine accesses into fewer memory transactions.

rows.question: Switch to distributed systems. Five replicas initially store tag zero and value zero. One writer assigns increasing integer tags, sends each tagged value to all replicas, and completes after three acknowledgments. Replicas retain only the highest tag received. A reader queries any three replicas and returns the highest-tagged value, without writing back. Messages may be delayed arbitrarily; replicas do not fail. Is this register linearizable? Give an explicit execution proving your answer, naming replicas and operation ordering. Then determine whether making each reader write its selected tagged value to three replicas before returning restores linearizability, including with concurrent readers and an unfinished write. Prove your conclusion.
rows.recognizedQuestion: switch to distributed systems five replicas initially store tag zero and value zero one writer assigns increasing integer tags sends each tagged value to all replicas and completes after three acknowledgements replicas retain only the highest tag received a reader queries any three replicas and returns the highest tagged value without writing back messages may be delayed arbitrarily replicas do not fail is this register linearizable give an explicit execution proving your answer naming replicas and operation ordering then determine whether making each reader write its selected tagged value to three replicas before returning restores linearizability including with concurrent readers and an unfinished write prove your conclusion
rows.answer:
No—the register without reader write-back is not linearizable. Writing each reader’s selected tagged value back to three replicas, and waiting for their acknowledgements, restores linearizability under the usual single-writer assumption that its writes are sequential.

Explicit counterexample: name the replicas A, B, C, D, E, initially storing (0, 0).
1. The writer invokes W1 with (1, 10), sending it to all five replicas. Deliver it only to A; delay the other messages. W1 remains unfinished because it has fewer than three acknowledgements.
2. Reader R1 queries A, B, C. Their replies are (1, 10), (0, 0), (0, 0), so R1 returns 10.
3. After R1 returns, reader R2 queries C, D, E. All reply (0, 0), so R2 returns 0.

For R1 to return 10, a linearization must include the pending W1 before R1. Real-time ordering requires R1 before R2, so R2 cannot return the older value 0. Leaving W1 out cannot explain R1 either. Thus no linearization exists.

With write-back, each reader first queries three replicas, selects the maximum tagged pair, then sends that pair to replicas and waits for acknowledgements from three before returning. Replicas must apply their highest-tag rule before acknowledging; if they already hold a higher tag, they retain it.

The key invariant is that every completed write or read leaves at least three replicas holding tags at least as large as that operation’s tag. Any later reader’s three-replica query intersects those three replicas. Because stored tags never decrease, that reader selects a tag at least as large. In particular, once a read returns a value from an unfinished write, later reads cannot revert to an older value.

Here is a linearization proof, including concurrent readers and unfinished writes. Give each read its selected tag. Order writes by their increasing tags, and place each read after the write that produced its tag and before the next write; order reads with equal tags consistently with real time. Include an unfinished write if a completed read returned its tag, and discard other unfinished operations as needed. Every returned noninitial pair originated from an invoked write, so this construction invents no values.

This order respects every real-time constraint:
• If a write completes before a read starts, quorum intersection makes the read’s tag at least that write’s tag.
• If a read completes before another read starts, its write-back quorum makes the later read’s tag at least its own.
• If a read completes before a write starts, its selected tag belongs to an already-invoked write, so the newly starting sequential writer’s tag is strictly greater.
• The single writer’s write order agrees with tag order.

Concurrent readers need not have increasing tags by completion time: overlapping operations can be ordered by their selected tags. Each read then returns exactly the latest preceding write’s value. That establishes linearizability, even when a read exposes an unfinished write.
